title: Opening: 'anhaga' and the poem
short: The poem opens on the 'anhaga', the solitary one, a man without a lord; it survives only in the Exeter Book.
body: The Wanderer, 115 lines, is copied in the Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols 76b-78a). The book was written c. 965-75 and given to Exeter by Bishop Leofric (d. 1072). The title is modern, from the first editions in the nineteenth century (Benjamin Thorpe printed the Exeter Book in 1842). 'Anhaga' (an 'one' + haga, related to hogian 'to think' or haga 'enclosure') means 'one who dwells or thinks alone'. Bosworth-Toller gives 'a recluse, solitarius'. The variant 'anhogan' returns at l. 40, so the word frames the first movement. In heroic society a man without lord and kin had no protection, no place in the hall and no one to speak for him. The poem turns that social loss into a meditation on the transience of the whole world. Most critics call it an 'elegy', but the label is modern and debated (Klinck).

title: are gebideð: waits for, or experiences, grace?
short: 'Gebidan' can mean 'wait for' or 'live to experience'; does the lonely man await God's mercy or already receive it?
body: 'Ar' means honour, favour, grace, here varied by 'metudes miltse' ('the Measurer's mercy', l. 2). 'Metod', 'measurer, ordainer', is an old poetic word for God or fate. The verb 'gebidan' with the genitive or accusative can mean 'to wait for' or 'to experience, live to see'. Read the first way, the opening is hopeful: the solitary often waits for grace, although he must toil at sea. Read the second way, it is a statement that he often does find it. Leslie and Mitchell-Robinson both discuss the double sense. The question it raises is answered only at the close, where 'are' returns: 'Wel bið þam þe him are seceð' (l. 114). Its concessive clause ('þeah þe he modcearig ... sceolde', 'although he, sad at heart, ... must') holds hope and hardship together from the first sentence.

title: lagulade, hreran mid hondum: the rowing exile
short: He must stir the frost-cold sea with his hands along the 'water-way': an image of exile as endless rowing.
body: 'Lagulad' (lagu 'sea, water' + lad 'way, course') is a poetic compound for the sea. 'Hreran mid hondum hrimcealde sæ' ('stir with his hands the rime-cold sea') pictures a man rowing. The detail of bare hands instead of oars stresses toil and isolation, and some critics read it in a Christian light as the exile's labour on the voyage of life. 'Wadan wræclastas' ('tread the tracks of exile') joins sea and land travel; 'wræclast' (wræc 'exile, misery' + last 'track') returns at l. 32 and in The Seafarer l. 57. The emphasis on cold (hrim, 'rime') runs through the whole poem and comes back at ll. 48 and 77. Note the h-alliteration of l. 4 ('hreran ... hondum ... hrimcealde').

title: Wyrd bið ful ared
short: 'Fate is wholly fixed' (or 'inexorable'): the first gnomic statement, closing the opening section.
body: 'Wyrd' (from weorþan 'to become') is 'what happens, event, fate'. In Christian Old English verse it is usually not a pagan goddess but the course of events under God, as in Boethian writing. 'Ared' is the past participle of arædan, 'to determine, decree', so 'fate is fully determined'. Some editors read it as 'inexorable', and the line's sense is debated. The short, closed half-line acts as a gnomic cadence, the first of many 'bið' sentences that generalise from experience (compare ll. 15, 65 ff., 106-110). Whether the half-line belongs to the narrator or to the wanderer is part of the larger crux of who speaks where. The word returns as 'wyrd seo mære' (l. 100) and 'wyrda gesceaft' (l. 107).

title: Swa cwæð eardstapa: who speaks?
short: The 'earth-stepper' is introduced as speaker; where his speech begins and ends, and how many voices there are, is a classic crux.
body: 'Eardstapa' (eard 'land, dwelling' + stapa 'stepper') occurs only here. 'Swa cwæð' can point backward (ll. 1-5 were his words) or forward (introducing ll. 8 ff.); editors usually take it forward, with an inset speech running at least from l. 8. A second frame at l. 111, 'Swa cwæð snottor on mode', raises the question of whether the wise man of ll. 88-110 is the same man grown old in wisdom or a second speaker. Pope's 1965 essay argued from the pronouns 'min' and 'sylf' for two speeches and an epilogue in each of this poem and The Seafarer; he later withdrew the argument ('Second Thoughts on the Interpretation of The Seafarer', Anglo-Saxon England 3, 1974). Most now read one consciousness passing from sorrow to wisdom, framed by a narrator (Leslie, Klinck). The quotation marks in the archive's text are an editor's choice, not the manuscript's. 'Winemæga hryre' ('the fall of dear kinsmen') names the grief.

title: uhtna gehwylce
short: 'Every dawn': 'uht' is the last part of the night before daybreak, when the sleepless man voices his sorrow alone.
body: 'Uht' (genitive plural 'uhtna') is the time just before dawn, the hour of the monastic office of nocturns or matins ('uhtsang'). 'Uhtna gehwylce', 'each of dawns', means 'every morning before light'. The same time of private grief appears in The Wife's Lament ('uhtceare', l. 7) and in Beowulf ('on uhtan', l. 126), where Grendel's slaughter is discovered. With 'ana' (alone) and 'cwiþan' ('to lament'), the line sets the man's speech as soliloquy: he has no one to whom he dare open his mind ('Nis nu cwicra nan', ll. 9-11).

title: indryhten þeaw: the ethic of silence
short: A noble man binds fast his 'mind-locker': the heroic ideal of restraint, set against the speaker's need to speak.
body: 'Indryhten' means 'very noble, lordly'; 'þeaw' is 'custom, practice'. The 'noble custom' is that a man should bind fast his 'ferðloca' (ferð 'spirit' + loca 'enclosure, lock') and keep his 'hordcofa' ('treasure-chamber'), whatever he thinks. 'Breostcofa' ('breast-chamber', l. 18) follows. These container kennings picture the mind as a locked chest. The restraint has a heroic side and a Stoic or Boethian side, much discussed. The irony is that the speaker breaks the rule even as he states it. Line 15 gives the reason: 'Ne mæg werig mod wyrde wiðstondan' ('a weary mind cannot withstand fate'). The image of binding recurs in fetters (l. 21), the bound waves (l. 24), and sorrow and sleep binding (l. 40).

title: goldwine; hrusan heolstre biwrah
short: 'My gold-friend', his lord, whom long ago 'the darkness of earth covered': the lord's death begins the exile.
body: 'Goldwine' (gold + wine 'friend') is a poetic word for a lord, the giver of gold who binds men to him by gifts. It returns at l. 35, and 'goldgiefan' appears in The Seafarer l. 83. 'Hrusan heolstre biwrah' means 'covered with the darkness (heolstor, 'hiding-place, darkness') of the earth'. 'Biwrah' has no expressed subject: the sense is that the darkness of earth covered his lord long ago, and the new clause 'ond ic hean þonan wod' ('and I, abject, went from there') begins the exile. Editors differ on whether to supply 'they' or 'one' as the agent of burial. 'Geara iu' ('long ago, of yore') stresses that the loss is old. 'Hean' (l. 23), 'abject, humbled', and 'wintercearig' ('winter-sad', l. 24) describe his state as he sets out over the sea.

title: ofer waþema gebind
short: 'Over the binding of the waves': the frozen sea is pictured as a binding, linking the outer world to the bound mind.
body: 'Waþum' or 'waþem' is a rare poetic word for wave or flood; 'gebind' is 'binding, fastening'. Most editors take the phrase as the sea locked by ice, or the waves' close-knit mass. The repetition at l. 57 ('ofer waþema gebind') frames the passage of dreams and visions. The phrase extends the poem's binding motif: the mind bound fast (ll. 13, 18), the heart in fetters (l. 21), sorrow and sleep binding the wretch (l. 40), and the hail-storm that binds the earth (l. 102, 'hrusan bindeð'). Critics often see binding as one of the poem's linking images.

title: sinces bryttan; meoduhealle
short: He seeks a 'dispenser of treasure', someone in a mead-hall who would know of 'his people' and comfort him.
body: 'Sinces brytta' ('distributor of treasure') is a traditional formula for a lord, also found in Beowulf (l. 607, of Hroðgar). 'Meoduheall' is the mead-hall, centre of the warband's life. 'Min mine wisse' is difficult. Most editors take 'mine' as 'love, affection' (myne), giving 'who would know my love' or 'who would show me affection'; other readings exist. 'Weman mid wynnum' (l. 29) is 'entice, entertain with joys'. The passage sums up what exile has lost: lord, hall, gift and fellowship. 'Selesecgas ond sincþege' (l. 34), hall-men and the receiving of treasure, are remembered next.

title: Warað hine wræclast, nales wunden gold
short: Exile, not twisted gold, holds him; a frozen spirit, not the glory of the earth: a pair of contrasts.
body: 'Warian' is 'to guard, occupy, hold'. The exile-track possesses him, not 'wunden gold' ('twisted gold', the rings a lord gives). The next line repeats the pattern: 'ferðloca freorig, nalæs foldan blæd' ('a frozen mind-locker, not the flourishing of the earth'). 'Blæd' ('glory, prosperity, breath') is a key word in both poems (Seafarer ll. 79, 88). The figure is a balanced antithesis, 'x not y', twice repeated, and shows how the poet uses variation. 'Ferðloca' (compare l. 13) is now cold, a physical image of grief.

title: The dream of the lord (ll. 41-44)
short: In sleep he seems to embrace and kiss his lord and lay head and hands on his knee, as when he enjoyed the gift-seat.
body: The dream shows a ceremony between lord and retainer: embracing and kissing the lord, laying hands and head on his knee. Scholars compare it with rituals of commendation and homage, in which a man put his hands in his lord's, though how far a real Anglo-Saxon ceremony lies behind it is debated. 'Giefstol' ('gift-seat', the throne from which gifts were given) recurs in Beowulf (l. 168). 'Breac' (brucan 'to enjoy, use') usually takes the genitive, but 'giefstolas' is an accusative plural, so the verb here governs the accusative. The happiness is felt in the mind ('þinceð him on mode') only. The sudden waking at l. 45 ('ðonne onwæcneð eft wineleas guma') makes the loss sharper.

title: fealwe wegas, baþian brimfuglas
short: Waking, he sees fallow waves, sea-birds bathing and spreading their wings, rime and snow falling with hail.
body: 'Fealu' ('fallow, dusky, yellowish-grey') describes the waves. The sea-birds (brimfuglas) bathe and spread their feathers ('brædan feþra'), a bleak replacement for the hall-company he dreamt of. 'Hreosan hrim ond snaw, hagle gemenged' ('rime and snow falling, mingled with hail') echoes the opening cold. Some read the birds in the light of The Seafarer's bird catalogue (ll. 19-25), where bird-cries replace men's laughter. The infinitives 'baþian ... brædan ... hreosan' after 'gesihð' ('sees') give the view as a series of present scenes.

title: The vision of kinsmen (ll. 50-55)
short: Memory of kinsmen passes through his mind; he greets them joyfully, but the 'companions of men' swim away: a famous crux.
body: The grammar and the referents of ll. 51-55 are disputed. 'Maga gemynd' ('memory of kinsmen') passes through his mind; he greets them 'gliwstafum' ('joyfully', literally 'with glee-staves'), and eagerly gazes on 'secga geseldan' ('companions of men'). Then 'Swimmað eft on weg!' ('they swim away again'). One reading makes the kinsmen a waking vision that fades. Another, followed by many editors, identifies the 'companions' with the sea-birds of l. 47, who seem to be his kin and then float off. 'Fleotendra ferð' ('the spirit of the floating ones') bring him few familiar words ('cuðra cwidegiedda'). Clemoes compared the passage with patristic ideas of the mind's wandering. 'Cearo bið geniwad' (l. 55) repeats l. 50's 'Sorg bið geniwad' and closes the section.

title: middangeard
short: 'Middle-earth': the world of men between heaven and hell, which is decaying and falling day by day.
body: 'Middangeard' (also 'middaneard') means 'the middle enclosure', the inhabited world. It is cognate with Old Norse 'Miðgarðr' and Gothic 'midjungards'. In Christian Old English it is simply 'the world', often set against heaven. Here it 'dreoseð ond fealleþ' ('droops and falls') every day. The idea that the world itself was ageing towards its end (the 'senectus mundi') was common in Christian writing from Cyprian and Augustine to Gregory the Great, and the poem shifts from personal grief to this general decline. Tolkien took his 'Middle-earth' from this word.

title: No man is wise until he has winters
short: No man becomes wise before he has had his share of winters: then follows a catalogue of the wise man's restraints.
body: 'Wintra dæl' ('a share of winters', i.e. years) makes experience the condition of wisdom. 'Wita sceal geþyldig' opens a list of the wise man's qualities: not too hot-hearted, nor too hasty of speech, nor too weak a warrior, nor too reckless, too fearful, too glad, too greedy for wealth, nor too eager to boast. The 'sceal' construction ('must, ought to be') is the mode of gnomic verse, as in Maxims I and II. The 'ne to ... ne to' series is a pattern of measure, close to the classical mean. 'Beot' (l. 70) is the warrior's formal vow, which must not be spoken before a man knows where his mind will turn. The passage marks the speaker's change from sorrow to wisdom.

title: The ruined walls (ll. 73-77)
short: The wise man foresees the world's end in the wind-blown, frost-covered walls now standing in various places across the earth.
body: 'Gæstlic' (l. 73) is 'ghostly, terrible', and the 'wela' ('wealth') of the world will stand waste. 'Missenlice' means 'in various places': the poet points to ruined buildings throughout the land. These were probably the Roman remains that Anglo-Saxons saw everywhere. 'Winde biwaune' ('wind-blown'), 'hrime bihrorene' ('covered, beset with frost'), 'hryðge þa ederas' ('the enclosures storm-beaten'). 'Woriað þa winsalo' ('the wine-halls crumble'). The lords lie dead and the proud troop has fallen beside the wall ('wlonc bi wealle'). Compare The Ruin, whose subject is a single such site.

title: The 'sum' catalogue and the beasts of battle
short: War took some; a bird bore one away; the grey wolf shared one with death; a sad-faced man hid one in a cave of earth.
body: The passage lists the ways the warriors died, with repeated 'sume ... sumne'. 'Sumne fugel oþbær ofer heanne holm' may mean a bird of prey or carrion carried one off over the deep sea. Some take the 'bird' as a ship or think it a kenning. 'Se hara wulf' ('the grey wolf') echoes the traditional 'beasts of battle' theme (wolf, eagle, raven), described by Magoun. The same 'sum' pattern structures The Fortunes of Men in the Exeter Book. 'Dreorighleor' ('sad-faced') describes the man who buried a comrade in an 'eorðscræf' ('earth-cave', grave).

title: eald enta geweorc
short: 'The ancient work of giants': the formula for Roman or prehistoric stone ruins, shared with The Ruin and Maxims II.
body: 'Ent' is 'giant'. 'Enta geweorc' ('work of giants') is a fixed formula in Old English verse for ancient buildings, especially Roman stone, which Anglo-Saxons did not build. Maxims II (ll. 1-2, after its opening 'Cyning sceal rice healdan') has: 'Ceastra beoð feorran gesyne, / orðanc enta geweorc' ('cities are visible from afar, the skilful work of giants'). The phrase is also in The Ruin (l. 2) and Beowulf (ll. 2717, 2774). The idea may draw on biblical giants before the Flood (Genesis 6:4), but scholars disagree on how far that is in mind. 'Ælda scyppend' (l. 85, 'creator of men') laid waste the dwelling until the old works stood empty, lacking the noise of citizens ('burgwara breahtma lease').

title: Hwær cwom mearg? The ubi sunt
short: 'Where has the horse gone? Where the young man?': the Old English poem's most famous use of the Latin 'ubi sunt' motif.
body: The questions 'Where has the horse gone, where the kinsman, where the treasure-giver? Where the seats of the feast? Where are the hall-joys?' follow the Latin 'ubi sunt qui ante nos fuerunt?' pattern. It is found in Isidore of Seville's Synonyma and in Old English homilies. J. E. Cross traced the sources and showed the poet's adaptation to heroic objects. 'Eala' ('alas, O') answers the questions with exclamations: the bright cup, the mailed warrior, the prince's glory. 'Hu seo þrag gewat, genap under nihthelm' ('how the time has passed, grown dark under the helmet of night'). The short half-lines and anaphora make the passage the emotional peak of the poem.

title: weal wundrum heah, wyrmlicum fah
short: A wall wondrously high, stained or decorated with serpent-shapes, stands where the beloved troop was.
body: 'Wyrmlic' means 'serpent-like' (wyrm 'serpent, worm'); 'fah' means 'stained, coloured, decorated'. The phrase may describe snake-like patterning in the stonework, whether carved decoration or marks of weathering; its exact sense is uncertain. 'Wundrum heah' ('wondrously high') shows awe at ancient stonework, as in The Ruin. The wall 'stondeð on laste' ('stands in the track, after') the dear company: a monument outlasting the people. The line cannot be tied to any known monument.

title: The winter storm (ll. 101-105)
short: Storms beat the rocky slopes, falling snow binds the earth, and night's shadow darkens and sends hail from the north.
body: 'Stanhleoþu' ('stone slopes') are battered by storms. 'Hrið' ('snowstorm') binds the earth, a final use of the binding image. 'Wintres woma' is 'the tumult of winter'. 'Nipeð nihtscua' ('the night-shadow darkens') is almost the same as The Seafarer l. 31 ('Nap nihtscua'). The shared language may point to common tradition, or one poet's knowledge of the other. 'Norþan' ('from the north') is the quarter of cold and, in some Christian writing, of evil. 'Hæleþum on andan' ('in enmity to men') makes nature hostile.

title: Her bið feoh læne: the 'loan' litany
short: Here wealth is lent, here friend is lent, here man is lent, here kinsman is lent: all this earth's frame becomes empty.
body: 'Læne' ('loaned, transitory', from lǣn 'loan') is the keyword. Four parallel half-lines name wealth, friend, man and kinsman, and the last line sums up: 'eal þis eorþan gesteal idel weorþeð' ('all this foundation of the earth will become void'). 'Idel' may echo the Vulgate's 'vanitas' (Ecclesiastes 1:2). Scholars often compare Hávamál st. 76-77 in the Poetic Edda: 'cattle die, kinsmen die', though in Hávamál fame survives. The Seafarer uses 'læne on londe' (l. 66).

title: Swa cwæð snottor on mode: the closing gnomic lines
short: The wise man sat apart in private meditation; the last lines turn to gnomic advice with longer, weightier half-lines.
body: 'Sundor' is 'apart' and 'run' is 'secret, counsel, mystery' (the same word as for a letter of the runic alphabet). 'Gesæt him sundor æt rune' means 'sat apart by himself in meditation'. Lines 112-115 are metrically heavy, with longer half-lines than the rest of the poem, and some metrists treat them as expanded (hypermetric) verse; the classification is less secure than in The Seafarer. Old English poets used such heavier lines for solemn or gnomic passages, as in the close of The Seafarer (see Bliss on hypermetric verses). 'Til' (l. 112) is 'good'. 'Treowe' is 'faith, loyalty'. A man should not reveal his 'torn' ('grief, anger') too quickly unless he knows the remedy ('bote') beforehand. This recalls the ethic of ll. 11-18.

anchor: Wel bið þam þe him are seceð
title: Wel bið þam þe him are seceð
short: 'It is well for him who seeks grace': the closing echo of 'are' resolves the opening, placing all security in heaven.
body: The final lines say it is well for the one who seeks grace ('ar'), comfort from the Father in heaven, 'þær us eal seo fæstnung stondeð' ('where all our security stands'). 'Fæstnung' ('fastness, firmness, security') contrasts with the 'læne' world. The word 'are' returns from l. 1, forming an envelope that many critics read as the poem's resolution. The heroic speaker's suffering leads to Christian consolation. Earlier critics took this frame as a monkish addition to a pagan core. Most now see the Christian conclusion as integral (Leslie, Klinck), though readers still debate how far it answers the grief.
